correctionsImplemented: Removed repeated gauze-stacking instruction from lesson, embedded check, diagram and matching bank concept.
Added prophylactic TIG 250 IU IM and qualified diagram vaccine thresholds as applying after a complete series.
Added tenth lesson, embedded case and diagram for liquid-bandage use and exclusions.
Namespaced all wound visual IDs to prevent collisions.
Added collagenase and hemostatic-powder lessons, diagrams, embedded checks and two assessment cases.
Added mupirocin ointment indication, dose, response check and formulation cautions; avoided blanket MRSA susceptibility claim.
Corrected baseline implication that collagenase directly attacks healthy tissue.
Distinguished mupirocin cream lesion limits and pediatric age from ointment.
Added OTC antibiotic use limits, sensitizer cautions and historical Cortisporin interpretation.
Qualified dressing-change interval in lesson and diagram: daily applies to ordinary bandages; specialized sheets follow product instructions and care plan.

Corrected implication that ischemia itself requires debridement: assess vascular supply first; explicitly preserve uninfected dry ischemic eschar pending restoration of flow, with urgent specialist care for acute infection or wet gangrene. Pressure-ulcer source scope stated.
Added missing safeguarding recognition from RxPrep page 558, with child injury-pattern examples supported by NICE and a local-procedure boundary.
discrepancies: Book dirty-wound booster wording greater than five years corrected by existing module to CDC five or more years.
RxPrep and MedlinePlus permit/recommend antibacterial ointment; AAD advises plain petrolatum without routine antibiotics for clean uncomplicated cuts. Module retains AAD approach.
Book collagenase described as most common debridement: do not teach that unsupported general ranking. Select by tissue and clinical assessment.
Book recommends uncovered drying if friction/contamination unlikely; retain AAD moist-covered care for uncomplicated wounds.
Book describes mupirocin as covering MRSA broadly; susceptibility cannot be assumed because resistance occurs.

Book calls Cortisporin ointment popular for superficial infection; retrieved Pfizer label is historical and indication requires steroid-responsive dermatosis with secondary infection, not routine wounds.
